column2: Your vassal, [FromFrom.GetTitledName], is concerned about [FromFrom.GetHerHis] non-inheriting daughters. [FromFrom.GetSheHeCap] asks you to consider them when looking for new vassals.
My humble request to gain land for [chosen_son.GetFirstName] was successful. I no longer have to worry about [chosen_son.GetHerHim].
Unfortunately, my Liege could not find it in [From.GetHerHis] heart to give my [chosen_son.GetSonDaughter] any land at this time.

My [chosen_son.GetSonDaughter] [chosen_son.GetFirstName] will now have [chosen_son.GetHerHis] own land! My Liege made sure to mention that I should remember this in the future when [From.GetSheHe] requires a favor in return.
I could use more good women.
What would be a suitable position for [moving_councillor.GetTitledName] on the Council?
[moving_councillor.GetSheHeCap] should be my [Root.GetChancellorName].
[moving_councillor.GetSheHeCap] should be my [Root.GetMarshalName].
[moving_councillor.GetSheHeCap] should be my [Root.GetTreasurerName].
[moving_councillor.GetSheHeCap] should be my [Root.GetSpymasterName].
[moving_councillor.GetSheHeCap] should be my [Root.GetLordSpiritualName].
I've changed my mind.

[aspiring_councillor.GetTitledFirstName] expresses [aspiring_councillor.GetHerHis] wish to have a seat on the Council. [aspiring_councillor.GetHerHisCap] contribution to the realm is significant and [aspiring_councillor.GetHerHis] military strength is not to be ignored, so including [aspiring_councillor.GetHerHim] in the Council may eliminate a potential future threat.
I'll see what I can do.
Knows there is hope.
We don't need you.
Is let down.
I would not bother you with such petty assignments.
Is flattered.
It has been long enough since [target_liege.GetTitledName] promised to make room for me on the council. I could remind [target_liege.GetHerHim] to keep [target_liege.GetHerHis] promise.
I'll be on the council in no time!
Remind [target_liege.GetTitledName] of [target_liege.GetHerHis] promise.
[target_liege.GetSheHeCap] probably has a good reason for delaying.

The request of [aspiring_councillor.GetTitledFirstName] for a Council position has been postponed long enough. [aspiring_councillor.GetSheHeCap] thinks it is questionable that [councillor_target.GetTitledFirstName] is allowed on the Council when [aspiring_councillor.GetSheHe] isn't.

The request of [aspiring_councillor.GetTitledFirstName] for a Council seat has been postponed long enough. Considering there is an open position, now would be the time to invite [aspiring_councillor.GetHerHim].
Yes, it's time for a change.
Welcome [aspiring_councillor.GetHerHim] to the Council.
The council is for important people.
Make up stories of slander by [councillor_target.GetTitledFirstName].
[aspiring_councillor.GetTitledFirstName] is angered.
My request to join the council of [target_liege.GetTitledName] will be considered.
Good news.
The answer regarding a position on the council of [target_liege.GetTitledName] was a definite no.
What a shame.

Although I didn't get a council position, I can rest assured that [target_liege.GetTitledName] knows I'm competent. In fact, [target_liege.GetSheHe] said that a council position would be a waste of my precious time.
I'm great.

[target_liege.GetTitledName] told me that [councillor_target.GetTitledName] has been slandering me! Of course my wise liege did not believe these lies, but the other councillors are worried, making it hard to give me a council position right now.
That snake!
Your vassal, [FromFrom.GetTitledName], is concerned about [FromFrom.GetHerHis] non-inheriting sons. [FromFrom.GetSheHeCap] asks you to consider them when looking for new vassals.
I could use more good men.
I can't give out land to anyone who asks.
[FromFrom.GetTitledFirstName] will remember this generosity.
My humble request to gain land for [chosen_son.GetFirstName] was successful. I no longer have to worry about him.
Great!
Unfortunately, my Liege could not find it in [From.GetHerHis] heart to give my son any land at this time.
Maybe next time.
My son [chosen_son.GetFirstName] will now have his own land! My Liege made sure to mention that I should remember this in the future when [From.GetSheHe] requires a favor in return.
Blessed be [From.GetHerHis] name.
No, I had something else in mind.
[From.GetSheHeCap] should be my Advisor.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] finds you in the yard, still sweating from the practice ground. "My [Root.GetLordLady], I have drilled your soldiers and led your patrols. When next you call the banners, give me a flank of my own to command. I will not waste a single life you place in my hands."
You will have your flank.
Wait your turn.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] lays out a roll of knives, bone-saws and bitter herbs before you. "Your court has no physician, my [Root.GetLordLady]. The barber who comes on market days bleeds men to death and calls it healing. Let me keep your household whole."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] lays a brace of pistols and a book of names on the table. "Corruption is patient, my [Root.GetLordLady], and your court has no one to watch for it. Give me the office of witch hunter, and nothing that crawls in the dark will reach your hall unseen."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has the hounds at heel and a stag's head at their feet. "The hunt at this court is a shambles, my [Root.GetLordLady]. The beaters are drunk and the dogs are half-wild. Make me master of the hunt and your guests will speak of your forests for years."

Candle flames lean towards [From.GetTitledFirstName] as [From.GetSheHe] speaks. "Every great house keeps a wizard, my [Root.GetLordLady], and the Winds blow strong around this one. Let me serve you openly, before someone less careful offers you the same."
The office is yours.
That is not yours to have.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] kneels before you, a borrowed lance at [From.GetHerHis] side. "My [Root.GetLordLady], I would ride out as a knight errant and prove myself in the Lady's sight. Give me leave and a purse for the road, and I will come home with spurs."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has been hiding it badly for years. The milk sours when [From.GetSheHe] is angry, the dogs will not sleep near [From.GetHerHim]. "My [Root.GetLordLady], the gift will not go away. Let me go and learn to master it from those who can teach me, before it masters me."

[From.GetTitledFirstName] has a letter from a guild-master far from here, offering [From.GetHerHim] a place among the apprentices. "Two years, perhaps three, my [Root.GetLordLady]. I would learn a trade this court has no one to teach. All I ask is your leave and a little coin for the road."
Go, and come back better.
I need you here.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] is back from [From.GetHerHis] years abroad, leaner and harder than when [From.GetSheHe] left, with new skills and new stories. [From.GetSheHeCap] kneels before you to take up [From.GetHerHis] old place at your court.
Welcome home.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] cannot sit still. "There is a war in every corner of the world but this one, my [Root.GetLordLady]. Free companies are hiring in Tilea, the north is burning, and the Border Princes are always fighting someone. Let me go and earn a name with my sword."
Go, and bring back stories.
Your sword is needed at home.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] is home, sunburnt and scarred, with a sword that has seen much use and a hundred tales of battles in lands you have only seen on maps. The court gathers round to hear them, and [From.GetSheHe] does not stint the telling.

A battered company banner arrives at your court with a letter from a captain you have never heard of. [From.GetTitledFirstName] died well, it says, in a foreign field, in a war nobody here will remember. The banner is all that came home.
Welcome back, and well done.
They chose their road.

At the feast [From.GetTitledFirstName] keeps your cup full and your table laughing. At the hunt [From.GetSheHe] rides at your side, and on the long evenings [From.GetSheHe] is always there with a story or a game. It is plain that [From.GetSheHe] wants your friendship, and does not much care who sees it.
Good company is rare at this court.
Their chatter tires me.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] stands before your throne in mourning black. "My kin lies in the ground, my [Root.GetLordLady], and everyone knows whose hand did it. [amb_kin_killer.GetTitledName] still walks free. I ask you for justice. If you will not give it, I will take it."
Seize the murderer.
I cannot touch [amb_kin_killer.GetHerHim].

[From.GetTitledFirstName] does not mince words. "My [Root.GetLordLady], I have served you well, but this is a small court, and [amb_great_court.GetTitledName] pays better and climbs higher. Give me a reason to stay, or I will take my talents to someone who values them."
Stay, and be paid as you deserve.
Go, then.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] unrolls a map covered in trade routes, river tolls and the names of merchant houses. "One cargo, my [Root.GetLordLady]. Wine down the river, furs up it, and every coin you lend me comes back with friends. All I need is a purse to start."
Here is your purse.
My gold stays with me.
[From.GetTitledFirstName] is back from the river ports with a heavy chest and a heavier purse. [From.GetSheHeCap] counts your grant back onto the table, and more besides, with a merchant's grin.
The cargo was sold, the purse was full, and [From.GetTitledFirstName] never came back. Word reaches you that [From.GetSheHe] has taken service at another court, and is spending your money there.
Gold well spent.
The thieving wretch.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] climbs onto a table in the middle of the feast, kicks over your ale and bellows for all the boyz to hear. "Oi! Dis boss is soft! 'E don't krump nuffin no more! I'm da biggest an' da 'ardest 'ere, an' I'm gonna prove it on 'is 'ead!"
Krump 'im!
Give 'im some teef to shut up.
Frow 'im to da squigs.

A servant in a stained livery waits for you in the stables, cap in hand and eyes on the door. The servant was in the household of [amb_rival.GetTitledName] until a week ago, and knows things: debts, letters, a door left unlocked at night. For a purse, all of it is yours.
Let every court hear of it.
Keep it for the right moment.
I do not deal in a servant's gossip.

A tracker comes out of the jungle with a broken spear and a tale. A carnosaur has made a hunting ground of the river crossings, and it has learned that men are slow. Whole villages have gone up into the trees to sleep.

A tracker comes down from the high passes with news of a wyvern. It has taken goats, then herdsmen, then a mule-train with its drivers, and its nest is a cave above the snow line, littered with bones.

A tracker comes in from the snow with frost in his beard. A troll of the deep north has crossed the ice, and it does not die when it is cut. The villages along the treeline have stopped going out after dark.

A tracker comes out of the deep woods with an empty quiver and a pale face. A manticore has made its lair in the old forest, and it has taken a woodcutter, a charcoal-burner and three of your best hounds.
Saddle the horses.
Not this one.
After days of tracking, the hunt finds it. The beast is bigger than the tales and hungrier, and it has turned at bay in a place of its own choosing. The hunters look to you.
Face it yourself.
Let the hunters bring it down.
If you fail, you are wounded and the beast escapes.
It comes for you and you hold your ground. When it is over the beast lies dead at your feet and the hunters are cheering your name. By nightfall the tale has grown in every tavern for twenty leagues.
A tale for the feasting hall.
Spears, nets and arrows bring the beast down while you watch from the saddle. It is dead, and it was your hunt, but everyone saw who held back.
It is dead, is it not?

Your beastmasters come back from the Mountains of Mourn with half the gnoblars they took and a story worth the loss. A Stonehorn herd grazes the high valleys, and one of the young bulls is wild enough for a proper Tyrant to break.
Rope it.
Too many gnoblars eaten already.
You wrestle the Stonehorn to the ground and break it to the saddle.
The Stonehorn throws you and runs. Try again in a year.

A priest of [Root.Religion.GetName] has heard what is said of you at court, and does not flinch from saying it to your face. "The gods see every sin, my [Root.GetLordLady], and they forgive those who truly repent. Confess, and I will set you a penance."
I will do penance.
My sins are my own affair.
The penance is long. Bread and water, prayer at every bell, the cold stone of the chapel floor under your knees. The priest watches you, and you know that what you put in is what you will get out.
Fast and pray.
Give alms in my place.
On the last morning of the penance something is gone from you that you did not know was so heavy. The old hunger does not come back. The priest only smiles.
The gods are merciful.
You last a week, then a day, then an hour. The old sin comes back as easily as breathing, and the priest leaves your hall without a word.
Next time.

You kneel all night in the chapel of the Lady with your sword laid on the altar before you. The candles burn down one by one. Somewhere near dawn the cold creeps into your bones and your eyes grow heavy.
Keep vigil until dawn.
Sleep, just for a moment.

[From.GetTitledFirstName] kneels before you in the chapel of the Lady, the dew of the vigil still on [From.GetHerHis] cloak. [From.GetSheHeCap] has ridden as a knight errant long enough, [From.GetSheHe] says, and asks to be raised a Knight of the Realm.
Rise, Knight of the Realm.
Not yet. Prove yourself.

In a dream you stand on the shore of a lake so still it holds the stars. A woman rises from the water, and her face is too bright to look on. She holds out a cup to you, and then she is gone, and you wake with the taste of cold water on your lips.
I will seek her, whatever it costs.
Only a dream.

The loremaster opens the Dammaz Kron on the great table and reads by lamplight. The grudge is old, the ink brown with years, and the wrong it records has never been paid for. Every beard in the hall is silent until the last word.
Let every beard remember it.
First we ask for weregild.

The stranger at court calls herself a merchant's widow, and nobody believes it. Perfume follows her from room to room, and her eyes are not quite the right colour. "You hold yourself back," she whispers. "Why? The Prince wants you to feel everything. Let me show you."
Show me everything.
Not tonight.

A scarred champion in brass and red walks into your hall without a by-your-leave and spits at your feet. "They say you hold back," he growls. "The Blood God does not care for those who hold back. Prove them wrong."
Blood for the Blood God!
Have him thrown out.

A plague-priest arrives with a cart of food so ripe it hums. He is jolly, round and covered in sores, and he insists on sharing. "Why so careful, friend? Grandfather loves us as we are. Eat, drink, let go a little!"
Pass the plate.
Another day, Father.

A sorcerer in a mask of shifting colours offers you a secret about one of your vassals. Half of it is a lie, he admits cheerfully, but which half? "Use it, and see what changes," he says. "Change is all the Architect asks."
Tell me, and I will use it.
I know a lie when I hear one.

You set the fifth skull on the others, and the world falls away. You stand at the foot of a mountain of skulls that rises beyond sight, and at its peak, on a throne of brass, something vast turns its head towards you. For one moment the Blood God knows your name.
Skulls for the Skull Throne!

The fever comes on you like a warm blanket. In your dreams you walk in a garden of rot and blossom, and a vast, kindly voice laughs and calls you child. When you wake, the sores on your skin feel like gifts.
Thank you, Grandfather.
Such a gift should be shared.

The foresters come in with torn coats and grim faces. A warherd of Beastmen has gathered in the deep woods, around a herdstone daubed with blood. They have burned a woodcutters' village already, and the braying can be heard at night from the edge of the trees.
Muster the hunt.
The foresters can deal with it.
The herd is scattered and its herdstone thrown down.
The herd ambushes the hunt in the trees. You are wounded and the Beastmen melt away.

The cauldrons have been bubbling since dawn. The feast is loud, long and very greasy, and the guest of honour is [From.GetTitledName], who is not enjoying it. The Great Maw is fed, and every gut in the hall rumbles in praise.
Pass da gut-salt.

The cooks have been planning it for months: seven courses, three pies, a roast big enough to feed a village and pudding to follow. All that is needed is the guests, and a feast is not great if fewer than five of your vassals sit at your table.
Send the invitations.
Too dear this year.
The feast lasts from second breakfast to long past supper. Every vassal comes, and every vassal leaves happy, holding their belly. They will be talking about it in the Moot for years.
The food is good, but too many places stand empty. A feast with so few guests is only a dinner, and the cooks are heartbroken.
Second breakfast for everyone!
The boyz are getting restless. There have been three fights in the camp this week, and someone krumped the cook. They want a proper scrap, the bigger the better, and they are looking at you.
Find 'em a fight!
Krump a few to calm 'em down.

The skink priests come to you with their crests flushed bright. [amb_sleeping_slann.GetTitledFirstName] has dreamed for a long age, and they believe the rite of waking may rouse the Mage-Priest, if enough devotion is spent on it.
Begin the rite.
Let the Old One dream.

For days the skinks chant in the temple, their voices rising with the smoke. At last the priests fall silent and look up at the vast, still figure of [amb_sleeping_slann.GetTitledFirstName] on its palanquin.
The Great Plan endures.
The slann's eyes open.
The slann sleeps on. The priests will try again.

A ranger comes in from the old roads, his beard full of dust. He has seen [amb_lost_hold.GetName]. The gates still stand, but grobi and worse walk the halls of our ancestors, and the hearths have been cold for centuries.
By my beard, we take it back.
The throng is not ready.

A coach with black horses comes through the mist to your gates. The old noble houses of Sylvania send word: they have no love for the living, and less for whoever holds their lands now. They will bend the knee to a von Carstein strong enough to take Sylvania.
Your lands are mine by right.
Then they will fear me.

The Grey Seer breathes the warpstone smoke and his eyes roll back. The Horned Rat has shown him a sign, he says, a seat empty on the Council of Thirteen. Who fills it is not yet decided. Some Warlords are already making offers.
Warpstone for the Seer's voice.
A pact with Warlord [amb_skaven_ally.GetFirstName].
The Seer lies, as Seers do.
Great Beast Trophy
The head, hide or horns of a great beast slain on the hunt, mounted above the hearth so that every guest asks how it was done.
A Pie for the Ages
The masterpiece of a halfling elder's great feast: a pie so fine that nobody dares cut it. It sits under glass in the hall, and it will be spoken of in the Moot for a hundred years.
A Rival's Secret
This character knows something about a rival that they would rather nobody knew.
Grudge Remembered
An old grudge has been read from the Book of Grudges, and every beard in the hold remembers it.
The Grey Seer's Favour
A Grey Seer has been paid in warpstone to speak well of this Warlord before the Council of Thirteen.

A priest of [Root.Religion.GetName] has walked your lands for a month, looking for the right ground. "There is a hill where the faithful already gather, my [Root.GetLordLady], but no roof over their heads. Give us the land and the stone, and I will raise a temple there in your name."
Build it, with my blessing and my gold.
Not on my land.

A captain back from the marches brings you a map. "Here, my [Root.GetLordLady]. A ford, a road and a ridge above both. Put a fort on that ridge and nobody comes through without your leave. Give me the gold and the men, and it will be done before the snows."

A captain of your garrisons brings you plans for a line of watchtowers. "Fires on the towers can carry word from the border to your hall in a night, my [Root.GetLordLady]. We have the forts already. All they need is the towers."
Raise it.
The walls we have will do.

A captain with a gold tooth and a salt-stained coat makes you an offer. "Every crew on this coast needs a cove where no excise man ever comes, and they will pay for it. Build us a hideout, and I will put in my share. You will have your cut of every prize that comes in."
Build it, and pay your share.
Pay me for the anchorage instead.

A rich widow in the white of Shallya comes before you. Her husband died of a fever no physician could cure, and she means to see that nobody else does. "I have gold, my [Root.GetLordLady], and the sisters have the skill. Give us a house to heal in, and the Mother of Mercy will remember you."
Gratefully accepted.
I will not have her priestesses meddling.

Your [Root.GetSpouseType] has found a chest of painted toy soldiers in the attic: pikemen, knights, cannon, even a little general on a horse. Before long the map table is covered with them, and you find yourself refighting the battles of your ancestors well into the night.
Just one more battle.
Word of your toy armies has spread. A dozen other lords keep painted regiments of their own, and one of them has invited you to a tournament of map-table generals. Your soldiers are ready. Are you?
I accept the challenge!
Put them back in the attic.

The tournament hall is full of grown men and women crouched over tables of painted soldiers, rolling dice and arguing over the rules. Your opponent has brought an army twice the size of yours, and a smug grin.
Advance the knights!
Your flank collapses, your general is surrounded and your opponent rolls a perfect six. Defeat. You learned more from this loss than from any victory, but that does not make it sting any less.
Sweep the board off the table!
Well played. Next time.
Your cavalry sweeps around the flank at just the right moment and the enemy line crumbles. The hall applauds. For a little while, at least, you are the greatest general in the land.
Victory!

Every night a gang of toughs brawls in the market square, and the watch is too frightened to stop them. You could put on a plain cloak, join the fight and see how well your lessons hold up against men who fight dirty.
Find me a plain cloak.
I have better things to do.
You wake in a gutter with a black eye, a split lip and no purse. Somewhere a ruffian is drinking your health with your own silver. You did learn a few new tricks, mostly the painful kind.
Find them and have them flogged.
I will fight better next time.

When the dust settles you are the last one standing in a ring of groaning ruffians. They buy you a drink, never guessing who you are, and teach you a few tricks no master-at-arms would ever show a lord.
Another round!

There is talk in the taverns of an old swordmaster who once served a great lord and now drinks himself to death in some backstreet hole. They say nobody has ever beaten him with a blade. Finding him will not be easy.
Find this man.
At last your agents find him, slumped over a table in a filthy tavern, owing money to every innkeeper in the quarter. He looks up at you with bloodshot eyes and asks who the devil you are.
This drunk can teach me nothing.
Pay his tab and ask him to teach me.
The old man laughs when you ask him to teach you. Then he looks at you more closely, sobers a little, and names his terms: you will do as he says, you will not complain, and you will not ask him why.
Agreed.
I will not take orders from a drunk.

For weeks the old man has you catching flies with a pair of kitchen tongs. You feel ridiculous. But one morning in the practice yard you find you can follow the point of a blade as easily as a fly, and your sword is always where it needs to be.
I begin to understand.
Now he makes you row a little boat up and down the river from dawn until dusk, and refuses to say why. Your hands are raw and your back is on fire.
Enough! Throw him in the river!
Keep rowing.

The old man watches you spar with the captain of your guard and nods once. "That is all I can teach you," he says, and walks away towards the nearest tavern. Your arms are strong now, and your blade is quick.
Thank you, master.
You spend a season drilling with the soldiers of your guard, sleeping in their barracks and eating their food. You learn more from the sergeants than from any book of war.
A good season's work.
You have spent the summer in the saddle, riding hard over rough country with your huntsmen and outriders. You can now turn a warhorse at the gallop with your knees alone.
A fine summer.

You have been reading of the campaigns of Sigmar Heldenhammer, who united the tribes of men and broke the greenskin hordes at Black Fire Pass. How did he hold the tribes together, and how did he choose his ground?

You have been reading the war-books of the High Kings, kept in the vaults since the Time of Woes: every march, every siege and every grudge of the War of Vengeance, written down in a cramped and careful hand.
You have been reading the histories of Tethlis the Slayer, who drove the Druchii from Ulthuan in a war of terrible patience. Every campaign is set down with an elf's eye for the long game.

Da shaman's been tellin' da story of Grimgor Ironhide again, da biggest an' 'ardest boss what ever lived. 'Ow he krumped da stunties, an' da 'umies, an' da pointy-ears, all in one summer. Dere's lessons in dere, if you listen.

The skalds have been singing of Asavar Kul, the Everchosen who led the tribes of the north to the gates of Kislev. Every verse is a lesson in how a warlord binds a hundred feuding tribes into one horde.
You have been studying the campaigns of the old kings of Nehekhara, written on tomb walls and scrolls of papyrus: how chariots broke the line, and how the dead may march where the living cannot.
There is much to learn here.
I must study this further.
Years of study have given you a deep understanding of the art of war. You see the battlefield as the great generals saw it, a board of ground and time and morale.
I have only begun.
There is little more to learn.
A new stratagem comes to me.
An inn on the high road has fallen on hard times. The innkeeper is selling for a song, and the road brings travellers enough. With a little money and a sharp eye, it could make you a tidy profit.
Buy the inn.
I am no innkeeper.
The inn is yours, and it needs a new name over the door. The regulars have been arguing about it for a week.
The Prancing Griffon.
The Drunken Halfling.
The Lord's Rest.
The Cask and Cudgel.
The cook has an idea: put more salt in the stew, and the customers will drink more ale. The question is how much salt.
A pinch.
A handful.
A sackful.
All the salt in the cellar!
The opening night is coming, and every inn needs some entertainment to draw the crowds. What will it be?
A priest to bless the house.
A wandering minstrel.
A juggler and fire-eater.
A greased pig. Whoever catches it keeps it.
The priest blesses the house, then the cellar, then every barrel in it, one cup at a time. By midnight he is singing hymns on the table and the crowd is singing with him.
Bless us all.
The minstrel knows every song in the Old World and a few that would make a Bretonnian knight blush. The crowd keeps him singing until dawn.
Another song!
The juggler drops a burning torch into the straw. Nobody is hurt, but the stable is a total loss, and he leaves without his fee.
At least it was memorable.
The greased pig bolts through the taproom, under the tables, over the bar and out through the kitchen, followed by half the village. Not one plate or cup survives.
Somebody catch that pig!
The stew is so salty that nobody can eat it. The customers leave thirsty and angry, and some of them do not pay.
Too much salt.
The salt works. The customers drink and drink, and the ale barrels empty faster than the cook can fill the stew pot.
Another barrel!
The inn is a success. A merchant offers you a fine price for it, more than you paid, and you leave knowing a great deal more about trade than when you started.
Sell the inn.
There is a patch of waste ground behind your hall that has been neglected for years. With some work it could be a fine garden, and gardening is said to teach patience and good management.
Fetch me a spade.
Leave it to the weeds.
After weeks of digging, planting and pruning, your garden is in full bloom. The cooks have fresh herbs, the court has a place to walk, and you have learned how much care growing things need.
A fine garden.
The tax rolls are a mess. Nobody knows how much land each village holds, or who owes what. A proper survey of your lands would take most of a year, but it could be worth it.
Begin the survey.
The old rolls will do.
The survey is done. Every field, mill and fishpond is written down, and you know your lands better than any of your stewards.
Very good.
You have spent the season going over the household accounts with your steward, line by line. You found three cooks who do not exist and a stable boy who is paid like a knight.
No more of that.
You cannot do everything yourself. You have spent the season learning to choose the right people and trust them with the work, and your lands are better run for it.
A wise lesson.
Your household servants have been stealing, quarrelling and sleeping on the job. You spend a season putting the household in order, and the court runs smoothly again.
That is better.

An old chest in the library holds a set of drawings in the manner of Leonardo of Miragliano: a flying machine of wood and canvas, with wings like a bat's. The notes in the margin swear that it will fly.
I must build it.
Madness.
For weeks you pore over the drawings with your carpenters, working out the angles of the wings and the weight of the frame. At last the machine stands in the courtyard, creaking in the wind.
Now it needs a pilot.
Somebody has to fly it. Who will it be?
My squire is light and brave.
The jester will do anything for a laugh.
The dog. Nobody will miss the dog.
Your squire leaps from the tower in the machine. For a glorious moment it glides, and then it drops like a stone into the moat. The squire crawls out, bruised and bleeding, but alive.
Somebody fetch a physician.
The jester leaps from the tower with a cheer. The machine flies, or at least falls very slowly, into the duck pond. The jester climbs out to roaring applause and takes a bow.
Bravo!
The dog refuses to go near the machine. While you are trying to coax it in, a gust of wind lifts the machine, and you with it, and drops you both into the courtyard.
Ow.
Your squire is healing well, and keeps telling everyone what it felt like to fly. With a few changes to the wings, the machine might do better next time.
Try again.
Burn the cursed thing.
The jester has been telling the story of the flight in every tavern in the city, getting better with each telling. People are calling it a wonder. A second attempt could make you famous.
Try again.
Once was enough.
While you mend, you study the wreckage of the machine. You still do not understand why it flew, but you understand a great deal more about why it fell.
Fascinating.
With new wings and a lighter frame, your squire climbs the tower once more. This time the machine soars out over the walls and lands gently in a field outside the town.
It flies!
The jester climbs into the rebuilt machine, waves to the crowd and leaps. This time it glides clear across the moat and lands in a haystack.
It flies!
The flying machine is the talk of the land. Scholars write to you from far away to ask about it, and you know more about wind and weight than any lord alive.
What next, I wonder?

In the library you find an old copy of the holy writ of [Root.Religion.GetName], annotated in the margins by a long-dead priest. His notes are sharp and wise, and they turn the familiar words into something new.
In the library you find an old copy of the Thousand Tales of the Sultans, its pages gilded and its margins full of the notes of a long-dead scholar. Behind every story is a lesson in statecraft.
In the vaults you find a scroll of the Books of the Dead, older than the mortuary cult itself. Its hieratic script tells of the gods, the afterlife and the duties of a king.
The loremaster brings you an old copy of the hold's records, the deeds of your ancestors set down in runes over a thousand years. Every page is a lesson from those who came before.
A wandering seer leaves you a book bound in skin, its pages full of visions of the Realm of Chaos. Most of it is madness. Some of it is not.
I will read it.
I have no time for books.
You close the book at last. It has given you much to think about, and you see the world a little differently than before.
Enlightening.
They say a hermit lives in a cave in the hills, a man who has spent fifty years thinking about the meaning of things. People travel for days to ask him a single question.
I will seek him out.
A madman in a cave.
After days of riding you reach the hills. The locals point you up a goat track and refuse to go any further.
Up we go.
An old man in rags appears on the path ahead of you. He looks at you for a long time, then turns and starts walking up the hill without a word.
Follow him.
He is just a beggar. Go home.
The hermit's cave is bare except for a fire and a few old books. He answers your questions with more questions, and you sit by his fire for days, talking and thinking.
I am beginning to understand.
When you leave, the hermit gives you no farewell. But the long ride home goes by in a moment, your head full of new thoughts.
Thank you, old man.

You have spent the season studying the ruins of the elder races: Dwarf bridges that still stand after three thousand years, and Elven towers whose stones fit together without mortar. How did they do it?
Remarkable.
You have been reading the philosophers of the old schools, who argued about the nature of the gods, the soul and the Winds of Magic. Much of it is nonsense, but some of it is not.
Food for thought.

You have spent many nights on the tower roof with an astrologer, charting the stars, the two moons and the wandering lights between them. Mannslieb keeps its course. Morrslieb does not, and that is worth knowing.
The heavens hold many secrets.
Two families in your lands have been feuding for three generations. Barns have burned, cattle have been stolen and last week a man was killed. If nobody stops it, it will end in a bloodbath.
Call them both before me.
Let them kill each other.
The two families stand on opposite sides of your hall, glaring at each other. One wrong word and the knives will come out.
Appeal to reason.
Flatter them.
We are all cousins here.
Your reasonable words fall on deaf ears. One of the patriarchs spits on the floor, and the other one draws a knife.
Guards!
You praise the honour and courage of both families. They puff out their chests, and the room calms a little.
Remind them of their duty.
Calm their tempers.
You point out that the families are related by a dozen marriages, as is everyone in this hall, including you. The patriarchs look at each other uncertainly.
You remind them that they owe their duty to you and to the realm, not to their feud. The younger men roll their eyes, and the shouting begins again.
The talk goes back and forth for hours. Tempers are rising again. You need to bring it to an end.
Threaten them with the gallows.
Shame them like children.
You threaten to hang the next man who lifts a hand. For a moment there is silence. Then somebody laughs, and a stool flies across the room.
You tell them that they are behaving like children squabbling over a toy, and that their grandfathers would be ashamed. The patriarchs look at their feet. Slowly, grudgingly, they shake hands.
That is more like it.
The meeting ends in a brawl. Your guards drag the two families apart, and the feud goes on. You learned a great deal about what not to say.
What a mess.
The feud is over. The two families feast together in your hall, and the patriarchs swear an oath of peace before the gods.
Peace at last.
You have taken to practising your speeches in front of a mirror, late at night when nobody can see. Your expression, your gestures, the pause before the important word: everything must be just right.
Again, from the top.
All that practice has paid off. Your speeches now hold the court spellbound, and even your enemies admit that you speak well.
Thank you, thank you.
A crowd has gathered in the castle yard. A man stands on the battlements, weeping and swaying in the wind. He has lost everything, they say, and means to throw himself off.
I will go up to him.
It is not my concern.
You climb to the battlements. The man turns to look at you, his face wet with tears. He is just out of reach.
Grab him!
Talk to him.
You lunge and catch him by the collar just as he steps off. Now he is dangling over the drop, kicking and screaming, and you are not sure how long you can hold on.
Let go.
Pull him in!
You let go. The man falls without a sound.
The crowd is silent as you come down from the battlements. Nobody meets your eyes. You will remember this for a long time.
I could not hold him.
With a great heave you drag him back over the battlements. He collapses at your feet, sobbing. The crowd below cheers.
You are safe now.
You talk to him quietly for a long time: about his family, his life, the things that still matter. At last he steps back from the edge and takes your hand.
Come inside.
You talk, but he does not hear you. He jumps. You will never know if there were words that could have saved him.
I tried.
You have spent the season listening to the town crier and the street preachers, learning how a voice can carry over a crowd and hold it.
Hear ye, hear ye!
You have spent the season with merchants and travellers from distant lands, learning their customs, their manners and a few words of their tongues.
The world is wide.
An old envoy who served at a dozen courts has been telling you stories of his career over many evenings: the treaties he signed, the wars he prevented and the lies he told.
A valuable education.

One of the ladies of the court has a jewelled necklace that she never stops showing off. It would be easy to steal it, and the practice would sharpen your wits. You would only need someone to take the blame.
Do it.
That would be wrong.
You slip into the lady's chamber at night and take the necklace. Now you need somewhere to hide it, where it will be found on somebody else.
In the cook's wife's apron.
Under a servant's mattress.
You slip the necklace into the apron of the cook's wife as she hurries past with a tray. She does not notice a thing.
Now we wait.
The theft is discovered. The lady is screaming, the guards are searching the castle, and the whole court is buzzing with rumours.
Search the kitchens!
The guards find the necklace in the cook's wife's apron. She swears she has never seen it before, but nobody believes her.
Take her away.
The cook's wife is dragged off to the dungeon, still weeping and protesting her innocence. The lady has her necklace back, and nobody suspects you. You feel a little cleverer, and a little colder.
It had to be someone.
Going through old papers, you find a note about the cook's wife who stole a necklace years ago. You had quite forgotten her. Is she still in the dungeon?
Hurry to the dungeons!
The cook's wife died in her cell long ago. The gaolers buried her in the castle midden, and nobody thought to tell you.
May the gods forgive me.
The cook's wife is still alive, a broken old woman who does not know you. You have her released, and she stumbles out into the daylight without a word.
Go, and forgive me.
You slip the necklace under the mattress of one of the servants while he is drinking in the kitchen.
Now we wait.
The theft is discovered. The lady is screaming, the guards are searching the castle, and the whole court is buzzing with rumours.
Search the servants' quarters!
The guards find the necklace under the servant's mattress. He swears he has never seen it before, but nobody believes him.
Take him away.
The servant is dragged off to the dungeon, still protesting his innocence. The lady has her necklace back, and nobody suspects you. You feel a little cleverer, and a little colder.
It had to be someone.
Going through old papers, you find a note about the servant who stole a necklace years ago. You had quite forgotten him. Is he still in the dungeon?
Hurry to the dungeons!
The servant died in his cell long ago. The gaolers buried him in the castle midden, and nobody thought to tell you.
May the gods forgive me.
The servant is still alive, a broken old man who does not know you. You have him released, and he stumbles out into the daylight without a word.
Go, and forgive me.
Servants hear everything and say nothing, at least not to their masters. If you dressed as one of them and sat in the kitchens for a while, who knows what you might learn?
Fetch me a servant's smock.
I am not sitting in the kitchens.
For weeks you scrub pots and listen. You learn who is sleeping with whom, who is stealing from whom, and who plots against whom. It is very instructive.
How interesting.
There is an old man in the city who was once the most feared spymaster in the land. He retired years ago and lives quietly now, but they say he has forgotten nothing.
I will pay him a visit.
Let sleeping spiders lie.
The old spymaster opens the door before you knock. He knows who you are, why you have come and what you had for breakfast. He invites you in.
Teach me.
The old man agrees to teach you, for a price and for the pleasure of it. "The first lesson," he says, "is that everyone lies. The second is that the lies tell you more than the truth."
I am listening.
Half a year of lessons is over. You can read a face like a letter now, and you see the plots and lies of the court as clearly as the old man does.
Thank you, old man.
You have spent the season with an apothecary who knows more about poisons than any honest man should, and about their antidotes too.
A useful knowledge.
You have spent the season with the captain of your bodyguard, learning how assassins think and how to stay alive when they come.
Better safe than sorry.
An old assassin, long retired, has been sharing his secrets with you over many evenings. How to move without being seen, how to wait, and when to strike.
Fascinating.
Your court has grown soft and decadent. The desert tribes still live as your ancestors did, hard and free. Perhaps you should spend some time among them.
I will go into the desert.
I am quite comfortable here.
You live among the tribes for a season, sleeping in tents, eating dates and drinking camel's milk. When you return, the luxuries of the palace seem strange and hollow.
The desert has changed me.
A band of desert raiders has been preying on the caravans. You could lead your guards against them yourself and show the court what a true son of Araby is made of.
Saddle my horse.
Send the guards.
I am too old for this.
At night you creep up on the bandit camp with your guards. The raiders are drinking around their fires, suspecting nothing.
Attack!
On second thought, let us go home.
Your guards burst into the camp, swords flashing in the firelight. The bandits scramble for their weapons.
Stay behind the guards.
Prepare stakes for the survivors.
Into the fray!
The bandits are dead or fled, and the caravans are safe again. Riding home in the dawn, bloodied and tired, you feel more alive than you have in years.
Glory to the Sultan!
Let their bodies be a warning.
Herdsmen swear they have seen a two-headed camel in the deep desert. It would be a fine trophy, and a hunt in the desert would do you good.
We hunt!
Two-headed camels do not exist.
Your hunting party rides out into the deep desert with falcons, hounds and enough water for a month.
Onward.
For days you ride over the dunes, but there is no sign of the beast. The herdsmen insist it is here somewhere.
Keep looking.
After weeks of searching you give up. There is no two-headed camel, and probably there never was.
Turn for home.
You come home burned by the sun, thin and hard, with no trophy at all. But the weeks in the desert have done what no physician could, and the palace seems very soft indeed.
It was never about the camel.
Instead of holding court in the palace, you have sent couriers to every corner of your lands with your orders. It is hard work, but your rule is felt everywhere.
Good.
You have stripped the palace of its silks, gold and dancers. The court grumbles, but your treasury is fuller and your people respect you more.
Luxury is weakness.
You have closed the pleasure-houses of the capital. The court is outraged, the priests are delighted, and your people see a ruler who means business.
No more idleness.
